lead: Mounting makes a file system visible at a directory called a mount point. The OS does not copy any data; it only links the existing storage into the global namespace. This mechanism lets local disks, USB sticks or remote shares such as NFS appear as ordinary directories, so applications can read and write files without knowing where the data really lives. It is used in desktops, servers and embedded devices that need to add storage on demand.
prereq: You need: basic file concepts (5.1) and directory hierarchy (5.2).

blocks.text: The kernel provides the system call mount(source, target, fstype, flags, data). source identifies the device or remote server, target is the absolute path of the mount point, fstype tells the kernel which driver to use, and flags control options such as read‑only. On success the call returns 0; on error it returns –1 and sets errno.

items: Create an empty directory that will become the mount point.
Invoke the mount system call (or the mount command) with appropriate arguments.
The VFS layer registers the new file system under the mount point.
Subsequent path look‑ups that reach the mount point are forwarded to the mounted file system.
Mounting does not move or duplicate files.
Multiple mount points can refer to the same source (bind mounts).
Unmounting with umount detaches the file system but leaves the data untouched.

blocks.where: FreeAfter is the remaining free space after copying; Total is the capacity of the mounted storage; Used is the amount already stored.

sections.h3: Mount point, VFS and local file systems

blocks.text: A mount point is any empty directory in the global namespace. The Virtual File System (VFS) is the kernel abstraction that presents a uniform API to all concrete file‑system drivers. When a mount occurs, the VFS inserts a pointer from the mount point to the root inode of the new file system. This lets the same pathname lookup code work for ext4, FAT, or any network file system.

items: The VFS caches directory entries to speed up look‑ups.
Permission checks are performed by the VFS before delegating to the specific driver.
See 5.4 for a deeper VFS description.

blocks.text: Network File System (NFS) allows a remote server to export a directory. Clients mount the export using a command such as mount -t nfs server:/shared /mnt. After mounting, the remote files appear under /mnt as if they were local. NFS uses the same VFS mechanisms, so permission, caching and locking behave identically to local mounts.

items: On the server, edit /etc/exports to list the directory and client permissions.
On the client, create a mount point and execute the NFS mount command.
Access files normally; reads and writes travel over the network.
NFS does not copy data to the client; only file metadata and data blocks travel on demand.
Performance depends on network latency and server load.
Security can be enhanced with Kerberos or by restricting client IPs.

spec.title: Mount integration
spec.aria: Mount integrates a file system into the VFS and can expose remote shares.

examples.question: A 4 GB USB stick is mounted at /media/usb. After copying a 200 MB video file, how much free space remains on the USB stick?
steps: Convert capacities to the same unit. 1 GB = 1024 MB, so 4 GB = 4096 MB.
FreeAfter = Total – Used = 4096 MB – 200 MB = 3896 MB.
Convert back to GB: 3896 MB ÷ 1024 MB/GB ≈ 3.8047 GB, which is reported as 3.8 GB.
examples.answer: Approximately 3.8 GB of free space remains.
examples.check:
total_gb = 4
used_mb = 200
free_mb = total_gb*1024 - used_mb
free_gb = free_mb/1024
print(round(free_gb,1))

traps: Assuming the mount command copies the whole file system to the local disk; mounting only links the existing storage.
Confusing the size of the USB (4 GB) with the amount of free space after copying; forgetting to convert GB to MB before subtraction.
Using the wrong unit for the video size (e.g., treating 200 MB as 200 GB) leads to a nonsensical free‑space result.
Thinking that unmounting deletes the data; it merely detaches the namespace entry.

quiz.a: An empty directory where a file system is attached to the global namespace.

quiz.q: Explain why mounting does not duplicate data on the local disk.
quiz.a: Mounting creates a VFS pointer to the existing storage; the data remains on its original device and is accessed through the pointer.

quiz.q: A 2 TB external HDD is mounted at /data. After storing 150 GB of logs, compute the remaining free space in TB (rounded to two decimals).
Write the command to mount an NFS export server:/share at /mnt as read‑only.
A system shows 0 B free space after mounting a 500 MB USB, even though the USB is empty. List three possible reasons.
quiz.a: 1) The mount point directory already contains files that mask the USB contents. 2) The USB was mounted read‑only and the OS reports the underlying device’s used space (e.g., hidden system partitions). 3) The mount failed silently and the path still refers to a local directory that is full.

quiz.q: Compare the security implications of mounting a remote NFS share versus copying the files locally.
quiz.a: NFS keeps data on the server; access is controlled by server‑side permissions and network security, but data travels over the network and can be intercepted. Copying locally removes network exposure but places data on the client, requiring local protection and possibly duplicating sensitive information.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, container orchestration platforms such as Kubernetes use dynamic volume mounts to attach storage to pods at runtime. Cloud providers expose block storage via iSCSI or NVMe over Fabrics, which the OS mounts just like local disks. Research continues on secure, zero‑trust file‑system mounting where authentication is embedded in the mount protocol. Next, explore distributed file systems like CephFS or GlusterFS to see how they extend the mount concept across many nodes.
